      G-9 AND G-13 LANDOWNERS’ REPLY BRIEF ON ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

       TO THE HONORABLE LINDA BRITE, DEE MARLO CHICO, AND LINDA J.

BURGESS          ADMINISTRATIVE                LAW       JUDGES         (ALJs),      STATE        OFFICE          OF

ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS (SOAH):

       COMES NOW, G-9 and G-13 Landowners, and files this Reply Brief on Issue Nos. 11

and 13 (Reply Brief) in the above-styled and numbered docket.

                                          I.    INTRODUCTION

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation

(collectively, Applicants) continue to maintain their position that the Import Path 2 Projects

(Projects) are “unquestionably” reliability projects.1 In Applicants’ Initial Brief on Issue Nos. 11

and 13, Applicants’ justification is focused primarily on the reliability need for all 765-kV

projects.2 However, the need for a group of projects that were studied together, not individually,




       1
           Applicants’ Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 at 6 (Oct. 7, 2026) (Applicants’ Brief).
       2
           Id. at 4-12.

                                                         2
 is not an answer to Preliminary Order Issue No. 11, whether or not the Import Parth 2 Projects on

an individual basis are necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards. As such,

Applicants continue to be unsuccessful in answering Preliminary Order Issue No. 11.

         In response to Preliminary Order Issue No. 13, what is the estimated congestion cost

savings for consumers that may result from the proposed transmission facilities considering both

current and future expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission levels,

Applicants reiterate that since these Projects are reliability projects, they are not required to

demonstrate congestion cost savings.3 Nonetheless, Applicants continue to respond to Preliminary

Order Issue No. 13 by generally discussing how all of the 765-kV projects are allegedly beneficial

to customers but remain silent as to any actual congestion cost savings related to Import Path 2

Projects based on factual data.4

         Under Commission Rules, in order to grant a certificate for a transmission project, need

must be determined.5 Specifically, need is determined based on the project being a reliability

project or an economic project.6 For an economic project, Applicants must present an “economic

cost-benefit study that analyzes the transmission project under a congestion cost savings test and

a production cost savings test.”7 If the project is a reliability project that is necessary to meet state




         3
             Id. at 16.
         4
             Id. at 16-18.
         5
             Public Utility Regulatory Act, Tex. Util. Code § 37.056; 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.101.
          6
             In addition to economic and reliability projects, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(iii) states “ERCOT may
recommend, and the commission may approve, a transmission project that is submitted as an economic or reliability
project and does not demonstrate sufficient economic savings or reliability benefits to merit approval on those grounds
if ERCOT determines the line would address a resiliency issue identified in the grid reliability and resiliency
assessment required by subparagraph (E) of this paragraph.” Here, no party alleges that the Projects would quality as
a resiliency project under this subsection, and thus, this is not at issue or being addressed herein.
         7
             16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i).

                                                          3
 and federal standards, then the economic cost-benefit study is not applicable.8 Throughout this

proceeding and in their Initial Brief on Issue Nos. 11 and 13, Applicants fail to demonstrate the

required need for the Projects as either a reliability or economic project. Consequently, the ALJs

correctly found that Applicants did not assert that the Import Path 2 Projects are necessary to meet

state or federal reliability standards, nor did Applicants include evidence quantifying the congested

cost savings.9 As such, the ALJs’ ultimate recommendation to deny the Application should be

upheld.

                           II.     PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NUMBER 11

          Applicants maintain their position in response to Preliminary Order Issue No. 11 that

Import Path 2 is necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards.10 However, despite

providing a directory of evidence, Applicants fail to provide sufficient justification that the Import

Path 2 Projects are necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards.11

          In an attempt to show that they do affirmatively answer Preliminary Order Issue No. 11,

Applicants assert that “[t]he existing system does not meet mandatory federal reliability standards,

and the Import Path 2 Projects, together with the other PBRP projects, are necessary to resolve

those violations.”12 In identifying violations, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT)

performed reliability assessments for the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) in accordance

with North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1,

the ERCOT Planning Guide, and the ERCOT Nodal Protocols.13 This shows the methodology


          8
               16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii).
          9
               SOAH Proposal for Decision with Memorandum at 149-50 (Aug. 20, 2026) (Proposal for Decision).
          10
               Applicants’ Brief at 4.
          11
               Id. at Exhibit A.
          12
               Id. at 6.
          13
               Id. at 7.

                                                          4
 ERCOT used in its studies, but it does not affirm that the Projects meet state and federal reliability

standards. Further, the assessments do not demonstrate that the Import Path 2 Projects would

resolve any of the violations. Instead, the studies were conducted using all 765-kV import paths,

not solely the Import Path 2 Projects. Therefore, any result that comes from the assessments does

not prove the need for Import Path 2 Projects specifically, nor how they specifically address any

violation.

       Similarly, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) Staff concludes that

“[t]he proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state and federal reliability

standards.”14 Commission Staff similarly relies on ERCOT’s reliability assessment in the PBRP

and the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans (RTPs) and the findings in those studies that

765-kV import paths are needed.15 Commission Staff’s analysis relies on results that include all

765-kV import paths and none that are specific to the Import Path 2 Projects.

       Moreover, Applicants contend that “[t]he record does not support the ad hoc removal of

any component of that [PBRP] plan, because no independent analysis or planning study shows that

the plan would still resolve the identified reliability issues without it.”16 The record does not show

this because there is no evidence of an analysis done without one of the 765-kV import paths.

Notably, Applicants confirmed that no analysis was done on any import path individually.17

Without such analysis, we do not know that all proposed 765-kV import paths are necessary. This

furthers the point that there is no evidence to support that the Projects are necessary to meet state

and federal standards.



       14
             Commission Staff’s Initial Brief on Remand at 2 (Oct. 7, 2026) (Staff’s Brief).
       15
             Id. at 2-3.
       16
             Applicants’ Brief at 11 (alteration in original).
       17
             Hearing on the Merits Monday, June 8, 2026 (HOM_V2) Tr. at 44:21-45:4 (Gurley Cross) (Jun. 8, 2026).

                                                             5
         Applicants further note that “the Commission has found that the PBRP establishes a

reliability need for the 765 kV import paths.”18 Applicants’ attempt to use previous approvals of

765-kV import paths as support for finding Import Path 2 meets state and federal standards is

unfounded and misleading. To begin with, a finding that there is a reliability need for a project is

different from a finding that the project is necessary to meet certain standards. Further, the

Commission’s Orders in the three dockets Applicants refer to are silent as to whether the

corresponding import path met the state and federal standard.19 Further, in two of the dockets,

Docket Nos. 59029 and 59336, the Administrative Law Judges did not address this issue in the

Proposal for Decision.20 In the remaining docket, Docket No. 59315, the Administrative Law

Judges found that the “765-kV import path option would . . . resolve reliability issues identified

under the NERC reliability standards, ERCOT protocols, and ERCOT planning criteria.”21 Again,

this is not a finding for an individual import path but for the plan as a whole. As the record reflects,

there is no evidence that any study was done on either of the Import Path 2 Projects individually.

As further noted by American Stewards of Liberty, “[t]he material difference between Docket

Nos. 59182 and 59475 and the other 765-kV proceedings is therefore not that the 59475 PFD

 uniquely failed to discuss PO Issues No. 11 and 13. The material difference is the result of the

need analysis. Here, unlike in the preceding PFDs, the SOAH ALJs concluded that Applicants

failed to establish need for the proposed project.”22

        The ALJs’ finding that there is a lack of need for the Import Path 2 Projects is grounded in

the evidence that circumstances which impacted the results of the PBRP and resulting 2024 and

2025 Regional Transmission Plans have changed.23 These changed circumstances include: 1)

changes to load-forecasting methodology that resulted in a reduction to projected load; 2) inflation

of projected load that was relied on in ERCOT’s studies; and 3) planning generation in the Permian

Basin.24 Due to these changed circumstances, the ALJs were correct in determining that Import

Path 2 is no longer needed.25

                       III.     PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NUMBER 13

        Applicants and Commission Staff both conclude that due to the Import Path 2 Projects

being reliability projects, the cost congestion savings test is not necessary.26 However, both

provide general discussion that the Projects may result in cost congestion savings.27 Neither

Applicants nor Commission Staff point to any data that states a numerical value for the congestion

cost savings which might result from the Import Path 2 Projects.28

(Oct. 7, 2026).
        23
             Proposal for Decision at 98-100.

Decision at 63-65, 72-82, 94-98).
        25
             Proposal for Decision at 98-100.
        26
             Applicants’ Brief at 16; Staff’s Brief at 3.
        27
             Applicants’ Brief at 16-18; Staff’s Brief at 3-4.
        28

                                                            7
        Applicants rely on ERCOT’s estimate that the 765-kV import paths will avoid $890 million

outage-related construction costs and provide customers with over $270 million in annual cost

savings compared to the alternative 345-kV, as well as ERCOT’s Independent Market Monitor’s

estimate that from 2020 through 2024 ratepayers paid over $10 billion for congestion costs to show

“the Import Path 2 Projects will result in savings across some cost categories when compared to a

345 kV alternative.”29 This, however, is not specific to the Import Path 2 Projects, nor does it

quantify the cost congestion savings which is what is being requested in Preliminary Order Issue

No. 13. Similarly, Commission Staff’s justification in finding that the Import Path 2 Projects may

provide some cost savings does not rely on any numerical data directly related to the Import Path

2 Projects and instead generalizes the savings.30

       Due to Applicants’ failure to provide any evidence quantifying congestion cost savings, an

order should be issued denying the Application and adopting the ALJs’ Proposal for Decision

finding that the record contains no evidence quantifying congestion cost savings.

                                       IV.   CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated above, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners respectfully request the

Administrative Law Judges maintain their findings and continue to propose denial of the

Applicants’ Application. The G-9 and G-13 Landowners further request any such relief to which

they have shown themselves entitled.

being reliability proj ects, the cost congestion savings test is not necessary.26 However, both

provide general discussion that the Projects may result in cost congestion savings.27 Neither

Applicants nor Commission Staff point to any data that states a numerical value for the congestion

cost savings which might result from the Import Path 2 Projects.28
